item.title: Trump Offers Putin Economic Relief in Hopes That Russia Will Return the Favor
item.description:
For years, critics of President Trump accused him of welcoming help from Russia to tilt elections in his favor. Now, with midterm elections in the United States two weeks away, Mr. Trump is explicitly seeking economic support from Russia.

A week ago, the Trump administration announced that it was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports. Late on Friday night, the White House released an executive order exempting Russia from a sanctions law that Congress passed last month. The moves were a last-ditch effort to lower the soaring gas prices in America that polls show are turning voters against Mr. Trump and Republican candidates.

Ukraine has frustrated Mr. Trump in recent months with its attacks on Russian oil refineries, which he blames for high global energy prices. Although the attacks have disrupted global energy supplies, oil prices have been climbing since the United States attacked Iran at the end of February, leading to violence across the Middle East and clogging the flow of oil through the Strait of Hormuz. Gas prices on Saturday averaged $4.31 a gallon in the United States, according to the AAA motor club, up nearly 45 percent since the start of the war.

The crumbling of years of work by the United States to put economic pressure on Russia to end its war in Ukraine raises questions about the Trump administration’s strategy to broker a peace deal. Mr. Trump’s executive order on Friday comes as the administration is pushing for Europe to resume buying more Russian gas, as part of the peace deal.

Mr. Trump’s waiver of the sanctions also casts doubt on why Congress passed legislation that was intended to punish Russia but made imposing the sanctions optional.

On Saturday, Mr. Trump’s decision was hailed by Russia and assailed by Ukraine.

“The suspension of some of the provisions of the Graham Act marks an important and truly historic moment,” said Kirill Dmitriev, who is Mr. Putin’s special envoy for investment and economic cooperation. “These provisions could have effectively brought all economic cooperation between Russia and the United States to a complete halt, inflicting serious damage primarily on the U.S. economy and global markets.”

President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine, who has maintained that Ukraine has a right to defend itself against Russia, condemned the sanctions relief for Russia and predicted that there would be more of that to come.

“I want to thank both Democrats and Republicans who supported his bill,” said Mr. Zelensky, who posted a photograph on social media of him with Senator Lindsey Graham, the South Carolina Republican who died in July after working for more than a year to build support for the legislation. “That was a major victory: this truly bipartisan support. And now, the decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me. And it definitely helps only the Russians.”

Skeptics of the law said that they were not surprised that Mr. Trump was ignoring the will of Congress. The sanctions in the law, which was named after Mr. Graham, were intended to target Russian officials, oligarchs and financial institutions. But the law also said that Mr. Trump could decline to impose the sanctions if he sent a letter to Congress explaining that they were not in the “national interest.”

The law also gave Mr. Trump new powers, which he has yet to deploy, to impose high tariffs on buyers of Russian energy products.

Some top Republican lawmakers who have recently run afoul of Mr. Trump criticized the president’s executive order on Saturday as letting President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia off the hook.

Senator John Cornyn, a Texas Republican, posted an article on social media that said, “Congress Must Investigate Trump’s Aid and Comfort to Putin.”

Senator Thom Tillis, a North Carolina Republican, called the decision “beyond irresponsible.”

“It’s unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every single day,” Mr. Tillis said in a social media post. “If the President wants to actually bring down energy prices, he can do it by solving the Iran problem, not by doing a solid for Vladimir Putin.”

But it appears that Congress has little recourse. Even when Congress mandates sanctions, the executive branch has broad discretion on whether to deploy them based on what it believes is best for national security.

“Presidents have always sort of bridled at congressionally mandated measures,” said Adam M. Smith, a former senior adviser to the director of the Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control in the Obama administration.

Mr. Smith said that he was surprised that Mr. Trump had opted against imposing any of the sanctions and noted that it gave the appearance that the president was turning away from Ukraine and toward Moscow.

“This plus the diesel deal will make some people concerned about where the president’s head is in this space,” Mr. Smith said.

Alex Zerden, the founder of the risk advisory firm Capitol Peak Strategies and a former official in the Treasury Department’s Office of Terrorism and Financial Intelligence, said that Mr. Trump appeared to be adhering to the sanctions law as it was written. He was perplexed by the political calculus of seeking economic assistance from Russia after Congress demonstrated bipartisan support for crippling Russia’s economy.

“The optics around this are confounding given the bipartisan and presidential support for the Lindsey Graham legislation,” Mr. Zerden said. “But the president maintains wide discretion with this Congress.”

During the Biden administration, the United States imposed more than a thousand sanctions on Russian targets and corralled allies to put a cap on the price of Russian oil. The Trump administration has been lenient in enforcing many of those sanctions and so far has only imposed new sanctions on Lukoil and Rosneft, Russia’s two largest oil companies.

The decision to offer Russia relief from sanctions because of fears about energy prices also represents an about-face for Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

At his confirmation hearing last year, Mr. Bessent said the Biden administration’s sanctions on Russia were not “fulsome” enough and described Russia’s invasion of Ukraine as one of the greatest tragedies of his adult life. He warned any Russian officials who were watching the Senate hearing that he would gladly ratchet up sanctions pressure to force Russia to the bargaining table.

“I believe that the previous administration was worried about raising U.S. energy prices during an election season,” Mr. Bessent said.

item.title: Elizabeth Holmes Film Opens to Over 2,000 Sold-Out Shows
item.description:
Two interesting things happened at this weekend’s box office: A documentary sold out theaters across the country, and Netflix reported box office numbers for the first time.

Yet neither of those movies topped the charts.

That prize went to Paramount’s “Street Fighter,” an action film based on a video game that is estimated to bring in $31 million for the weekend.

Still, it is Nathan Fielder’s confounding documentary on Elizabeth Holmes, “You Can See Everything,” that has captured the cultural zeitgeist. Released on 855 screens, with over 2,000 sold-out shows, the nearly three-hour documentary follows Ms. Holmes, both a month before entering federal prison for crimes related to her medical technology company, Theranos, and two years into her sentence. It grossed an estimated $15 million from Friday through Sunday, making it one of the largest openings this century for a movie debuting on less than 1,000 screens. It will expand to wide release next weekend.

Co-directed by Lance Oppenheim (“Primetime”), it’s the highest grossing nonmusical documentary to hit the big screen since Michael Moore’s “Fahrenheit 9/11” from 2004. Reviews have been rapturous, with critics calling it “unmissable” and “off the charts bonkers.” Prognosticators are already imagining a world where it lands a best-picture nomination, which would be a first for a documentary.

On a much smaller, but no less significant, scale, Netflix began its 45-day theatrical release for the Spanish-language film “La Bola Negra,” which it acquired at the Cannes Film Festival. Debuting on four screens in New York and Los Angeles, the film is getting the streaming giant’s longest ever exclusive theatrical release. And it marks the first time a Netflix movie will be subject to the scrutiny that comes with box office reporting.

For the weekend, it grossed an estimated $277,500, with a per-screen average of $69,375, the second-highest per-screen average for a non-English language film. Directed by Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo (known colloquially as “Los Javis”), the well-reviewed, two-hour-35-minute multigenerational Spanish epic centered on the lives of gay men nabbed the audience award at the Toronto International Film Festival. It may also be Netflix’s strongest Oscar contender in years.

In comparison, “Fjord,” Neon’s international film from Romania — and one of “La Bola Negra’s” biggest competitors for recognition in the awards race for Best International Film — opened last weekend on four screens to $124,000.

Netflix intends to expand the screening of “La Bola Negra” to additional cities in the next few weekends before going to up to 300 screens on Nov. 6. It will debut on Netflix on Dec. 2.

The film is the first of a few Netflix films that are getting an exclusive theatrical release ahead of debuts on the streaming service. On Nov. 25, “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,” a prequel of sorts to “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” with a script from Quentin Tarantino and directed by David Fincher, will debut on IMAX screens for a two-week exclusive run. The studio will give Greta Gerwig’s Narnia adventure, “The Magician’s Nephew” a wide theatrical release in early February before it goes to Netflix on April 2.

Netflix has been clear that it’s a streaming company first and is interested in giving theatrical releases only to films that can play in theaters without hurting their performances on the service. (Many industry watchers believe that movies that open in theaters first perform better on streaming services.)

To the Netflix co-chief executive Ted Sarandos, the two types of movies he’s willing take a chance on are art house films and family films, which he says do a lot of repeat business. “So we said let’s take those two and treat them different,” he said last month at the Bloomberg Screentime conference. “We have relatively low expectations that will add much to the financial outcome of the film itself.”

But theater owners, who have long wanted Netflix to put its movies in theaters as the major studios do, are cautiously optimistic.

“I think it’s great that they’re finally joining us on how the industry is run in the U.S.,” said Luis Olloqui, chief executive Cinépolis USA, a luxury theater chain. His company won’t be screening “La Bola Negra” or “Cliff Booth.” It would rather turn its two IMAX screens over to the “Hunger Games” movie coming in November. His company is still deciding whether to screen the Peter Berg war film “Mosquito Bowl.” Netflix is giving the film an exclusive theatrical release later this year, though one with a shorter window than the others.

But it’s Ms. Gerwig’s epic “Narnia” movie in February that Mr. Olloqui says the entire exhibition community is excited about since it’s a big exclusive wide release for a movie that has the potential to be a blockbuster.

“We’re all looking forward to it,” he said. “It’s very good for the movie, for the whole industry and for the clients to have it on the big screen, as it should be seen.”

Other films released this weekend included “Whalefall,” an action film from Disney’s Fox division about a scuba diver being swallowed by a sperm whale. Made for $60 million, the movie opened to an estimated $7.5 million and will struggle to earn its production costs back. A remake of “Sense and Sensibility” from Focus Features opened to $6.7 million. The film, which has already grossed $8 million overseas, scored well with both critics and audiences.

“Musk,” the nearly four-hour documentary on the Tesla and SpaceX founder Elon Musk, expanded to 472 screens in North America on its second weekend. The film’s per-screen average dropped to $650 from $17,330 last weekend, and its total gross after two weeks stands at close to $400,000.

The film’s distributor, Bleecker Street, says that the box office performance has been negatively affected by advertising repression on social media sites. In particular, the company’s ability to promote the film on TikTok was permanently suspended on Friday.

In response, a spokesperson for U.S. TikTok said on Sunday that the restriction on the film’s ad account was an error and that the account is now in good standing, with the ability to post advertisements restored. But the spokesperson added that any ad published must comply with company policies and that the social media platform did not allow political advertising.

item.title: China’s Export Boom Fuels Growth Despite Slump at Home
item.description:
Surging exports and the industrial production needed to sustain them kept China’s economy growing over the past three months, even as consumer spending stagnated and investment plunged.

China’s National Bureau of Statistics announced on Monday that gross domestic product grew 1.2 percent from the second quarter of this year. If that pace continues for a year, the Chinese economy will expand at an annual rate of about 4.9 percent.

The figures are an improvement from the 4.3 percent growth rate China reported from April through June. The economy was 4.5 percent larger in the third quarter than in the same quarter last year, suggesting that the country remains on track to meet its official target of 4.5 to 5 percent growth this year.

But many Western economists have become increasingly skeptical of China’s official statistics, particularly as Beijing has gradually stopped publishing thousands of narrowly focused data sets that had provided separate checks on broader economic figures. Independent estimates of recent growth have generally been only half to two-thirds as high as the official numbers.

China’s export boom from July through September, which further widened its enormous trade surplus with the rest of the world, helped shield the economy from a much worse outcome. Exports in September rose at their fastest year-over-year pace since July 2010, excluding months distorted by the timing of Lunar New Year celebrations, which disrupt factory production for weeks.

At home, the picture was far bleaker.

Retail sales were exceptionally weak throughout the third quarter, though September sales rebounded somewhat from a particularly bad August. A prolonged housing market crash, which has driven existing-home prices down roughly 40 percent since 2021, has wiped out much of the middle class’s savings and left millions of households reluctant to spend.

Sales of cars and other durable goods, including household appliances, have plummeted.

An extensive government program of trade-in subsidies, introduced in the summer of 2024 and continued through the end of 2025, encouraged households to make purchases they might otherwise have waited to buy. Many consumers have little reason to now replace their cars or appliances. But car sales have fallen below their pre-subsidy levels, as rising unemployment further undermined consumer confidence.

Investment has also slumped, particularly in real estate construction. Even infrastructure spending, long a mainstay of Chinese economic growth, has faltered. The collapse of many real estate developers has devastated local governments’ revenue from land leases, historically their largest source of funds for building roads, bridges, rail lines and other public works.

The result is an economy increasingly dependent on selling goods abroad, even as domestic demand deteriorates.

“China basically must keep global exports markets open for this system to continue to operate,” said Logan Wright, a partner at Rhodium Group, a research firm.

Mao Shengyong, the spokesman and deputy commissioner of the National Bureau of Statistics, said at a news conference in Beijing on Monday: “We should be aware that the international environment is complex and volatile, the issue of insufficient domestic demand remains prominent, and the foundation for steady economic growth still needs to be consolidated.”

The stark divide between China’s industrial strength and its struggling domestic economy is visible in cities like Nanjing, a former capital in central China, and Guangzhou, the commercial hub of southeastern China.

Nanjing South Railway Station is a colossal monument to China’s world-leading high-speed rail system. Some of the country’s busiest north-south rail lines intersect there with major east-west lines that stretch inland from Shanghai along the Yangtze River.

But just a 10-minute walk away, a nearly deserted three-story shopping mall offers a strikingly different portrait of the economy. Its arches painted in golden and burnt sienna hues, the mall was almost devoid of shoppers last week. Many storefronts were shuttered. The few businesses still operating had only one employee, or sometimes no one at all, relying instead on China’s ubiquitous security cameras to deter theft.

In one nearly empty store, cans of tile grout and other flooring supplies sat piled up, with no customers in sight. “Our sales have fallen by around 30 to 50 percent over the past two years,” said the store owner, who gave his family name, Zheng. “It’s the same across all industries, not just ours.”

At a nearby wood paneling shop, sales have nearly halved over the past five years.

“The real estate market hasn’t recovered, and that’s affecting all kinds of businesses; the Nanjing economy was built on real estate,” said the shop owner, who gave her family name, Liu.

While businesses tied to the housing market struggle, some of China’s strongest manufacturers are benefiting from the global rush to build data centers, including in the United States. Exports of everything from power management equipment to steel racks for computer servers have soared.

Yet even as exports jumped 36 percent in September from a year earlier, Beijing remains wary of letting the country’s weak currency regain much of its previous value. The government has also been cautious about scaling back more than $300 billion a year in tax breaks for exporters. That support is essential for many lower-tech manufacturers, like the garment makers, which face tariffs in overseas markets and consumers unwilling to spend at home.

In Guangzhou, Tang Xiangfa, who has run a zipper shop for more than a decade, has watched his sales tumble.

“If business gets so bad that we can’t keep going, then we’ll have no choice but to switch to another business,” he said. “If we can keep going, we’ll continue.”

Ruoxin Zhang contributed research.

item.title: The VW Bus, Now Electrified, Keeps on Truckin’
item.description:
With two-tone paint featuring Sunshine Yellow body panels, the electric Volkswagen Type 2 (colloquially known as the Microbus) I recently experienced was not built for introverts.

This vintage bus, newly fitted out with electric power (its original rear-mounted engine made no more than 53 horsepower) caused a lot of heads to swivel on a leisurely tour of Bergen County, N.J., near the Hudson River and the New York border.

Kindred Motorworks, based on Mare Island, Calif. (a former U.S. Navy shipyard north of San Francisco), is betting that it can succeed with an electric version of the beloved Microbus that’s ready for modern traffic.

Volkswagen’s nostalgia-inducing hippie wagon is back, in two zero-emission flavors: Kindred’s “restomod” vintage model, with a robust E.V. drivetrain, along with a new, retro-styled electric bus from the company itself.

Kindred is betting that what affluent E.V. customers really want, instead of Volkswagen’s slow-selling ID. Buzz, is the return of the first-generation split-window Microbus, extant from 1950 to 1967, albeit with a lot more power. Those customers, the company said, also appreciate such modern touches as heated seats, air conditioning and connectivity to Apple CarPlay and Android Auto they wouldn’t get in a traditionally restored bus.

Along for the ride in New Jersey were Greg Clark, then the chief commercial officer at Kindred, and Basil Elbanna, a test engineer. “Customers want authenticity,” Mr. Clark said. “There are plenty of companies restoring Microbuses to 100 percent perfection.” But, he added, “don’t even think of climbing hills with one. So, a modern E.V. version makes every sense in the world.”

Mr. Elbanna added that there were plenty of primitive aspects to the original Microbus, including a heater that worked (or, in most cases, didn’t) by simply wrapping “heater boxes” around the hot exhaust headers and blowing air through them.

Kindred, under its founder and chief executive, Rob Howard (a former technology executive), started out building all manner of so-called restomods, collector cars with modern comforts, and working to make the process more efficient. The company began delivering old Ford Broncos in both gas and electric versions in 2025. But Mr. Elbanna said the new E.V. Microbus, introduced this year, “is our hero product.”

He said, “It solves the only bad thing about the original car — the lack of power.” According to Mr. Clark, Kindred’s goal is to produce approximately 12 electric buses the first year, and then scale up to perhaps 50 annually. The conversion remains a slow process, involving 1,500 work hours, and the end product won’t come cheap. The price is $275,000.

Our 1966 Microbus in New Jersey featured the treasured 23-window configuration ($100,000 to $200,000 for pristine, top-of-the-line examples), but Mr. Elbanna said it hadn’t started out that way. Kindred typically begins the restoration process with less-valuable models and converts them up.

Climbing into the Microbus one first encounters a nearly horizontal, original-type steering wheel (and no, there’s no airbag). The antique tiller represents the biggest hurdle to piloting these countercultural icons. What looks like a manual shifter is essentially an automatic, since the always-available torque in E.V.s makes a plethora of forward speeds unnecessary.

Behind the relatively plush leather-clad front seats, the bus features seating that wraps around a detachable table, and a row of storage cabinets. The passenger seat swivels to face the table, which would have made placement of an aftermarket center console (with cup holders!) somewhat difficult.

The bus took off without drama, and proved a capable cruiser on the Palisades Parkway. Drivers in modern S.U.V.s were probably astonished to see themselves passed by a slowpoke Microbus. The Grayback electric drivetrain (named after a submarine built on Mare Island) is similar in Kindred’s Microbus and Bronco, though the former makes do with just one 294-horsepower motor. That’s plenty of oomph for a Microbus, and with a 74-kilowatt-hour battery pack under the floor the Kindred is endowed with up to 200 miles of cruising range.

The bus has little in the way of aerodynamics, so there’s quite a bit of wind noise, drowning out any whine from the electric motor. The vibration level isn’t too bad, but it’s enough to blur the small period-appropriate rearview mirrors. The driver sits right over the front wheels, with no crumple zone or hood to impede, so the view forward is excellent, as is the maneuverability, but a major focus on occupant safety was in the future when this bus was made.

The original bus, with a lot of weight in the rear, tended to oversteer, but having the battery pack underneath in the Kindred version helps matters considerably. It’s no sports car, but it’s fun to drive for errands.

And that’s where Mr. Clark sees his market. “The vast majority will be used for buzzing around town, going to the beach or visiting the vacation home with the grandkids,” he said. Women are well represented among the buyers, he added.

Of course, Volkswagen has the retro ID. Buzz, which is off to a slow start in the U.S. market. With updated but evocative styling in a long-wheelbase, three-row version with available all-wheel drive, the Buzz that went on sale in the American market in 2024 can zoom to 60 m.p.h. in as little as six seconds. But the long-anticipated electric bus experienced many delays reaching the market and arrived with a daunting $59,995 starting price. (Kindred’s mortgage-like cost may make VW’s price tag easier to swallow.)

Volkswagen skipped the 2026 model year for the U.S. owing to excess inventory, but is planning to come back in 2027 for the 2028 model year with Tesla’s NACS charging onboard. There will also be a “Tourer” camper version with an “overnight mode” to save battery power while camping (or is it glamping?), a foldout mattress and other outdoor amenities. Campers are part of the Microbus heritage.

Other markets can buy cheaper ID. Buzz versions with two rows of seats, and utility configurations have done very well in Europe. Ryan Gavin, product manager for the ID. Buzz, said VW had sold a modest 12,000-plus vehicles in the United States and Canada since the introduction.

“We could not have had worse timing,” he said. “We started sales right after the 2024 election, which resulted in the loss of the $7,500 federal income tax credit for E.V.s and disinvestment in the charging infrastructure. Plus, there was a cultural vibe shift that didn’t favor our update of a super-happy hippie van from the past.”

In July, the VW Group announced a consolidation and restructuring that will cut as much as 50 percent of its global lineup. In the meantime, both of these electric Volkswagens will have to contend with a tepid U.S. market for E.V.s. Electric cars were at or approaching or price parity with gas cars around 2025, said S&P Global Mobility, but the loss of that federal income tax credit was a blow.

A 2025 ID. Buzz, when experienced as a test car, had many qualities the Kindred E.V. lacked, including very quiet operation, all-wheel drive, copious storage (including cup holders), an airbag in the conventional steering wheel, abundant safety technology, and three-row seating with electrically operated sliding doors and rear hatch. But it lacked the quirkiness and virtuous economy that makes the original Microbus so charming. A more extroverted interior would help.

Mr. Gavin of VW says he welcomes conversion companies like Kindred. “We love seeing what VW owners, both recent and far in the past, are able to do with their cars,” he said. “We relate. Our biggest challenge for this project was adapting an icon.”

]]>

item.title: U.S. Political Money Funnels to Indian Bots to Lure Voters
item.description:
The videos appeared across social media in August before the closely contested Democratic primary for the U.S. Senate in Michigan. They showed people on the street expressing support for one of the candidates, Representative Haley Stevens, and discussing the issues that mattered most to them.

“Definitely affordability,” a woman who identified herself as Darlene from Detroit said in one video. “You’ve got to make sure people can make a living.”

At least three dozen videos in all appeared on X, Facebook, Threads and Instagram, where they were viewed millions of times. While they projected grass roots authenticity, there was little authentic about how they reached voters.

The accounts that spread them were based not in Michigan but mostly in India, according to two research organizations that track disinformation. Posters were paid $1 to $5 for each thousand views to sway an election on the other side of the world, misleading viewers to think the content was organic to their feeds on social media.

These types of videos have become a prominent new feature of American political campaigns, spreading inorganic content on social media to attract voters without disclosing the ties to candidates or their proxies.

They resemble tactics — and even use some of the same for-hire bot networks — that Russia and China have employed to try to influence American voters.

Similar efforts to create and spread inauthentic content have cropped up in other elections, including the mayoral primary in Los Angeles last summer, the race for governor in California and a get-out-the-vote campaign targeting Black voters in Ohio.

“The whole information ecosystem right now is based in some sense on blurring the lines between who are legitimate sources, if you want to call them that, and shadier, more nefarious sources,” said Daniel Weiner, a senior director at the Brennan Center for Justice, a voting rights organization. “The idea that the ordinary voter or consumer of information can always tell the difference — I think we’ve seen, time and time again, that’s not really the case.”

The videos reflect a shift in campaign tactics as prospective voters tune out traditional political outreach in an increasingly fractured, algorithmically driven media environment online.

In response, candidates across the political spectrum are seeking to reach voters in new ways beyond paid ads.

Some have honed their own accounts on video-first platforms online, especially TikTok and Instagram. Others have also recruited influencers — the famous and the not famous at all — to spread the word online at a small fraction of the cost of ads on Facebook or YouTube.

The source of the interviews in Michigan — and the money behind them — remains a mystery. So does the identity of the people who appear in the videos, who after brief interviews give only first names and hometowns.

One of the Instagram accounts involved in spreading the videos, Energetic Humor, is operated by a man in Mumbai, India, who in an interview identified himself as Ayush Jain. He said he had made about $15 on each of 40 posts he published on different accounts he controlled.

While the creators of the videos are unknown, the campaign appears likely to have been tied to one of a number of political action committees or other groups that sought to help Ms. Stevens defeat her top rival in the race, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed. He prevailed in the primary on Aug. 4, which was closer than polls had predicted, and will face the Republican nominee, Mike Rogers, in November.

The videos do not appear to be deepfakes, realistic images fabricated with artificial intelligence tools. Some showed recognizable streetscapes in Detroit. In others, though, services that detect A.I. flagged possible indications of manipulation or fabrication.

The videos were not attack ads. The comments mostly focused on political issues and praise for Ms. Stevens, though at least one singled out criticism of Dr. El-Sayed from a right-leaning online news organization over tax return disclosures.

Ms. Stevens, who will remain in her House seat until January, did not respond to requests for comment. Caitlin Legacki, a strategist and campaign consultant for the Stevens campaign until stepping down in July, said she had seen the videos but was certain the campaign had nothing to do with them.

The campaign’s filings with the Federal Election Commission disclose payments to three companies for media services. Two did not respond to requests for comment; the other declined to comment.

The Stevens campaign also received about $60 million in backing from half a dozen outside groups, according to data from AdImpact, a media tracking firm.

“You don’t have to be a superconspiratorial person to think of various interests that would not want somebody with his politics in the United States Senate,” Ms. Legacki said, referring to Dr. El-Sayed and his political positions.

Dr. El-Sayed’s campaign declined to comment on the videos.

The Michigan primary video campaign was first identified by Antibot4navalny, a prominent group of anonymous volunteers who have exposed Russian trolling efforts online, including new attempts to undercut Democrats this election cycle. The group tracked 28 accounts on X that shared the videos as part of a coordinated, for-hire campaign that generated more than seven million views on the platform.

Researchers at Clemson University’s Media Forensics Hub identified additional accounts that spread the content on X and the other platforms, including Facebook, Instagram and Threads, all owned by Meta.

Those included accounts that the center’s researchers had detected before in influence campaigns involving Chinese bot networks.

One of the Instagram accounts that spread the Michigan videos has a user bio in Mandarin.

Some of the accounts also reposted content by Michael Carbonara, a Republican in Florida who in August lost a primary race for a House seat, according to Darren Linvill, a co-founder of Clemson’s research lab. (Mr. Carbonara did not respond to a request for comment.)

The accounts used for the Michigan videos typically promoted content intended to induce mindless clicks, then suddenly shifted to specific political content. Mr. Jain in Mumbai said his contract had required him to post the videos for a minimum of 30 days. They have since been deleted.

Since the primary, Mr. Jain’s Energetic Humor account has posted dozens of clips from cartoons like “The Simpsons” and “Family Guy.” Those are interspersed with other political posts, including more recent ones supporting the Republican candidate for governor in California, Steve Hilton.

Another mocks soaring gasoline prices with a meme from “The Sopranos” — a theme being pushed by Democratic candidates. The post featuring Mr. Hilton includes a note in the comments saying his campaign had paid for it.

The company that paid Mr. Jain was Lumina Clippers. It is one of a plethora in the United States and abroad that offer to boost attention online using bot accounts. The clientele in this marketplace can include political candidates as easily as consumer products, health and beauty aids, or cryptocurrencies.

Lumina Clippers is registered in Bethlehem, Pa.; has a telephone number in the United Arab Emirates; and is run by an Irishman living in Portugal, Rhys McKay.

In an interview, Mr. McKay acknowledged his company’s role in spreading the videos, including hiring Mr. Jain and dozens of others like him. Mr. McKay declined to identify who had hired him to do so, as well as the cost of the contract, citing client confidentiality.

The impact of the videos in Michigan is difficult to measure with certainty, but Mr. McKay said internet users had grown tired of political ads and simply swiped past them.

The interviews of voters was the kind of content that people online found more engaging.

People, he said, “resent being force-fed content.”

item.title: ‘A Ticking Time Bomb’: An Economic Crisis Looms in Indonesia
item.description:
Novri Putra graduated from college in Jakarta last year with a degree in information technology and a modest ambition: a stable job.

He had every reason to believe that he was on track. When he entered college in 2018, Indonesia’s economy was flourishing. Its tech sector was booming and demand for software engineers was surging.

Those days are over. Today, Mr. Novri, 28, works for a tech company — not as a web developer, as he had hoped, but as a motorcycle taxi driver making about $220 a month.

“My parents scold me almost every day,” Mr. Novri said. “Honestly, they probably feel a sense of shame that their child went to college and ended up as a motorcycle taxi driver.”

Mr. Novri’s predicament speaks to a greater malaise in Indonesia, where an economy once known for its stability is showing alarming signs of strain.

Like its Southeast Asian neighbors, Indonesia is struggling with the fallout from the war in Iran and American tariffs. Inflation is rising and fuel shortages are spreading across multiple cities. But government policies under President Prabowo Subianto are compounding its troubles, weakening institutions and raising doubts about the country’s economic management.

On Friday, the country was roiled after MSCI, an influential index provider, warned it could drop Indonesia from its benchmark indexes, which guide investment decisions by fund managers worldwide. The country’s stocks suffered their biggest one-day plunge since the 1998 Asian financial crisis, falling by more than 11 percent. On Monday, the selling continued with a nearly 4 percent decline.

A decade ago, this country of nearly 290 million people was seen as a reliable safe haven as other emerging markets battled currency collapses and hyperinflation. Although it still reports strong economic growth, other indicators tell a different story.

The number of people considered middle class has shrunk by about 19 percent from its peak. Lower-class savings rates have plummeted. Youth unemployment hovers around 17 percent, among the highest rates in Asia.

Experts now warn that Indonesia is facing its most combustible moment since 1998, when an economic collapse forced the ouster of the former dictator Suharto.

“It is a ticking time bomb,” said Ferry Latuhihin, the former chief economist at Bank International Indonesia who served on an expert council advising Mr. Prabowo before his administration took office.

“No one predicted in 1997 that Suharto would fall because of the malfunction of the economy,” he said. “The same story, I believe, might happen to this government.”

Experts do not expect the market turmoil to spread to regional neighbors. Phillip Wool, head of research and portfolio management at Rayliant, an investment firm based in California that manages $17 billion in assets, said MSCI’s concerns were specific to Indonesia, which accounts for a small share of most emerging-markets investors’ portfolios.

“It’s a risk that’s really isolated to Indonesia,” he said.

But the economic ripple effects may extend further. Indonesia is the world’s largest producer of palm oil, nickel and Barbie dolls and a major exporter of thermal coal, copper and natural gas. An economic crash could disrupt electric-vehicle production and drive up global prices for food, consumer goods and energy.

A study in July led by Indonesia’s former finance minister found that the erosion of the middle class correlates with more frequent protests. In August 2025, demonstrations erupted nationwide over the death of a ride-sharing driver at a protest and rising unemployment and inflation.

Thomas Lembong, Indonesia’s former trade minister, warned that too many things are going wrong at once.

“We’re getting closer and closer to the edge of the abyss,” he said.

Indonesia’s economic turmoil has revealed weaknesses that Mr. Prabowo’s policies have done little to address.

High oil prices and rising U.S. interest rates have drained dollars from Indonesia and put pressure on its currency, the rupiah. Indonesia is highly exposed because it relies heavily on imports of essential goods.

Yet Mr. Prabowo is doubling down on populist programs that are straining Indonesia’s budget and alarming investors. One example is a free-meal program for more than 80 million students, estimated to cost up to $30 billion a year.

Harris Turino, an opposition lawmaker, said that suspending the program for just three days would free up enough money to pay college fees for 20,000 students for a decade.

Investors are also questioning the Prabowo government’s transparency. A former general and Suharto’s former son-in-law, Mr. Prabowo has moved to nationalize assets and use a newly established sovereign wealth fund to advance his agenda.

MSCI cited “a lack of meaningful enforcement” against market manipulation for its warning on Thursday. The index provider said it had started consultations on whether to downgrade Indonesia’s market classification to the same category as countries facing international sanctions or prolonged economic turmoil.

The message was clear: Indonesia was now considered an unreliable investment.

The MSCI announcement came after two credit ratings agencies, Moody’s and Fitch, downgraded Indonesia’s outlook to negative from stable earlier this year. Indonesia’s exchange has lost nearly 40 percent of its value this year, making it one of the world’s worst-performing stock markets. On Friday, the rupiah breached the psychologically important threshold of 18,000 to the dollar.

Last month, Mr. Prabowo bristled when reporters pressed him about the credit downgrades.

“Are we really supposed to let a few people determine our rating? I mean, shouldn’t we be the ones deciding?” he said. “We are a sovereign country. How can people sitting far away, who know nothing about us, give us a rating?”

Until the pandemic, international investors praised Indonesia for adhering to a strict fiscal deficit ceiling that kept government debt at around 30 percent of its economy. Its central bank was also regarded as independent and stable.

The sudden departures of key policymakers who helped build Indonesia’s reputation have unnerved investors. In September 2025, Mr. Prabowo removed Sri Mulyani, the finance minister seen as a steady hand under former President Joko Widodo. In July, the widely respected central bank governor abruptly resigned.

Economists are also questioning the reliability of Indonesia’s official statistics.

Capital Economics, an independent research firm, said faster growth in last year’s fourth quarter was “hard to square” with other data showing a weakening economy.

On the ground, many Indonesians say the economy already feels as if it is in recession.

Muhammad Fajar, a 21-year-old street vendor in downtown Jakarta, said he has applied for jobs at more than 100 companies with no response. He graduated three years ago from a vocational high school specializing in motorcycle engineering and said he was willing to take almost any job.

“I do feel I’ve moved down a class,” said Mr. Fajar, as he flipped meatball skewers on his grill.

Reinita Hariyanti, founder of an organization that helps professionals navigate job displacement, said layoffs once confined to tech start-ups have spread to other sectors. Formal jobs are shrinking, she said, even as more people look for work.

Even the employed are looking to cut back.

Cut Erika Ananda Fatimah, a 52-year-old university lecturer who makes about $820 a month, said she had given up many of the things she once enjoyed: Starbucks coffees, trips to Malaysia, shopping for clothes and going to the gym. Such cutbacks spell trouble for an economy that relies heavily on consumer spending.

“I hope things will get better and that the middle class can once again feel that there is a possibility of moving up,” she said.

On a recent Friday, Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa, Indonesia’s finance minister, attributed the middle class’s plight to previous officials who, he said, had been content with economic growth of just 5 percent.

He said Moody’s and Fitch were swayed by “negative sentiment promoted by nongovernment parties,” rather than focusing on Indonesia’s growth and debt levels. He noted that S&P Global and a Chinese rating agency both gave Indonesia a stable outlook.

Mr. Purbaya said he met with MSCI officials in March. It was “useless, they didn’t believe me,” he said.

“Not many people really understand what is happening in the economy, including those economists who used to criticize me,” he added. “The most important thing is that I can rebuff them by the real economic result.”

He never got the chance. Three days after the interview, he was fired by phone without explanation. Hours later, Mr. Prabowo swore in Indonesia’s third finance minister in two years.

Muktita Suhartono contributed reporting.

item.title: Art Basel Las Vegas? The Fight Over Miami Beach’s Fair
item.description:
Goodbye Art Basel Miami Beach, hello Art Basel Las Vegas?

That was the blunt warning from one of the world’s leading art fairs to Miami Beach officials last week, suggesting the event might move to Nevada if the city didn’t drastically reduce the fees it was charging for the use of its Convention Center every December.

Questions of whether Art Basel would leave its longtime South Florida home, where the fair has been held since 2002, arrived on the heels of 18 months of deadlocked negotiation between MCH Group, the Swiss-based owner of five international Art Basel fairs, and Miami Beach over a plan to keep Basel in place.

The sticking point, as discussed by city officials at a public meeting last Wednesday before a vote on a revised contract, was Art Basel’s demand to essentially halve the nearly $1 million annual rent the fair had previously paid to Miami Beach.

“If this deal doesn’t move forward, is Art Basel ready to walk from Miami Beach?” City Commissioner David Suarez asked Noah Horowitz, the chief executive of Art Basel.

“We would by necessity re-examine our position in Miami Beach,” Horowitz replied.

Ultimately, officials were unwilling to test whether Basel was bluffing. Miami Beach Mayor Steven Meiner and the commissioners voted 6-1 to approve a new five-year contract with Art Basel through 2031 — with a reduction in its annual rent from nearly $1 million to $500,000.

Andrea Zappia, the chief executive of MCH Group, discussed the possible relocation to Las Vegas last December during a visit to the home of Norman Braman, the billionaire Miami auto dealer and philanthropist who is widely credited with convincing MCH to debut a Miami Beach edition of its fair.

In an interview on Friday, Braman said that Zappia, who was accompanied by MCH’s chief communications and corporate affairs officer Frederic Michel, told him that unless Basel received a huge reduction of its rent, it would leave Miami Beach for Las Vegas once its current contract, which ran through December, expired.

The transformational impact of Art Basel has been undeniable in ways that have extended far beyond Miami Art Week, the dizzying array of pop-up shows, special events and satellite fairs that engulfs the area during Art Basel, which runs this year from Dec. 2-6.

Indeed, a city once considered simply a louche adult playground is now credibly touting itself as a year-round global cultural destination. That’s not to mention the annual $60 million direct economic impact of Basel, its 80,000 attendees and its accompanying events, according to city tourism officials.

But if MCH was hoping that all of this would convince Braman to intercede in the contract negotiations on its behalf, it was mistaken. The auto dealership magnate considered any rent reduction to be “offensive,” he said, and talk of relocation to be a bluff. (When asked about the visit, a spokeswoman for Art Basel, May Mansour, said that organization did not comment on specifics of contractual negotiations.)

Under the new deal, Art Basel won additional credits for police, fire and EMT services from the city, which bring the total annual savings for the fair to about $650,000. Competing art fairs are also now prohibited from renting the Convention Center for 30 days before and 30 days after Basel’s own fair, which gained veto power over any events in public parks or on the beach that fall within a surrounding “Art Basel zone” of roughly one square mile surrounding the center.

The discussion leading up to the vote, which was televised locally, grew heated at times. Commissioner Suarez, an open skeptic of the revised contract, called Braman and then held his phone up to his dais microphone.

Braman told the meeting that he was all in favor of the fair continuing, but that he believed that better terms for the city could still be negotiated. He pointed to MCH’s announcement in 2020 that the media mogul James Murdoch had become an anchor shareholder by investing about $80 million, as well as the company’s most recent public financial statement, which reported profits of nearly $22 million for the first six months of 2026, much of which was credited to the success of its Art Basel fairs.

In that light, neither Murdoch nor MCH needed the city’s helping hand, Braman insisted.

“It’s not up to taxpayers to subsidize private enterprise,” he said.

Besides, if Basel did leave, Braman added, “I have been in touch with people — the new owners of the Frieze art fair — who would come into the city of Miami Beach in a moment’s notice and take over the entire time that Art Basel now has.”

(Belinda Bowring, a spokeswoman for MARI, Frieze’s parent company, called Braman’s claim “completely untrue.”)

As for Art Basel’s own perspective, Horowitz, its chief executive, offered a bracing reflection on the troubled state of the art world business. He told attendees at the meeting that MCH’s recent profits followed years of “extraordinary losses in which MCH almost faced insolvency. They took in a large investment from James Murdoch’s Lupa Systems family office to stabilize the business.”

Moreover, Horowitz said, Art Basel’s fairs — in Basel, Switzerland; Hong Kong; Miami Beach; Paris; and Qatar — were “currently facing a cyclical downturn, the likes of which we haven’t seen since the launch of Art Basel Miami Beach in the early 2000s.”

Horowitz added that, with the market forcing so many galleries to cut expenses by limiting their fair participation, or to close altogether, Art Basel Miami Beach had chosen to shrink rather than to fill itself with subpar galleries. (Last year 283 galleries were represented in the fair’s main sectors, compared with the 250 that are expected this December.)

In light of Horowitz’s bleak economic forecast, another city commissioner, Joe Magazine, said he was not inclined to test whether Basel was bluffing about moving.

“It’s not a game of chicken I’m willing to play,” he said.

Magazine joined the 6-1 majority in approving the new contract, with only Commissioner Suarez dissenting.
